status: Every source below was fetched on 2026-11-03 and the quote found on the page. Drinks are treats, not hydration plans.

petmd_cranberries.title: Can Dogs Eat Cranberries?
petmd_cranberries.quote: Yes, dogs can have a little bit of cranberry juice—as long as the cranberry juice is 100% juice with no sugar added.

akc_cranberries.title: Can Dogs Eat Cranberries?
akc_cranberries.quote: Prepared cranberry dishes are also risky, as are any grape/cranberry juice blends and cranberry dishes with sugar or alcohol.

akc_watermelon.title: Can Dogs Eat Watermelon?
akc_watermelon.quote: Seedless, rind-free frozen watermelon chunks can be a safe and refreshing treat, particularly during warmer months.

petmd_blueberries.title: Can Dogs Eat Blueberries?
petmd_blueberries.quote: Yes, frozen blueberries are safe for most dogs and can be a refreshing treat during warm weather.

petmd_chicken.title: Can Dogs Eat Chicken?
petmd_chicken.quote: Onion and garlic are both common additives found in canned chicken broth and—again—these are toxic to dogs.

petmd_yogurt.title: Can Dogs Eat Yogurt?
petmd_yogurt.quote: Never give your dog a yogurt containing xylitol, which can be fatal.

petmd_pumpkin.title: Can Dogs Eat Pumpkin?
petmd_pumpkin.quote: Yes, dogs can eat pumpkin puree as long as it's 100% pumpkin with no added ingredients.

pph_xylitol.title: Is Xylitol Dangerous for Dogs
pph_xylitol.quote: Sugar-free substitutes such as xylitol are extremely toxic to dogs.

aspca_people_foods.title: People Foods to Avoid Feeding Your Pets
aspca_people_foods.quote: Since dogs are not able to process tartaric acid, exposure to grapes/raisins can lead to kidney damage.

pph_caffeine.title: Caffeine Are Toxic To Pets
pph_caffeine.quote: Ingestion of unused coffee grounds or beans, tea bags, or supplements could cause serious toxicity in dogs or cats.

akc_treats.title: How Many Treats Can Your Dog Have?
akc_treats.quote: Treats should make up no more than 10% of your dog's daily calories

petmd_cats_milk.title: Can Cats Drink Milk?
petmd_cats_milk.quote: Unfortunately, most cats do develop lactose intolerance as they mature.

petmd_cats_water.title: Why Your Cat Won't Drink Water and What to Do
petmd_cats_water.quote: Cats love running water and a pet water fountain is a great way to help encourage them to drink.

treat.text: A sip is a treat. Water first, and treats stay under 10% of the day.

never.text: Never: grape or raisin juice, anything sugar-free (xylitol), coffee, tea, alcohol, onion or garlic broth.

catsMilk.text: No milk for cats: most adult cats are lactose intolerant.

sips.name: Cranberry splash
sips.how: A bowl of water with a splash of 100% cranberry juice, no sugar added. A tablespoon in a cup of water is plenty.
sips.note: Not juice cocktail, not grape-cranberry blends.

sips.name: Watermelon ice
sips.how: Seedless, rind-free watermelon frozen in cubes. One cube in the water bowl on a hot day.

sips.name: Blueberry cubes
sips.how: A few blueberries frozen inside water ice cubes. Drop one in the bowl.

sips.name: Broth cooler
sips.how: Homemade or plain low-sodium chicken broth with no onion or garlic, chilled or frozen in cubes.
sips.note: Read the label: canned broth often has onion and garlic.

sips.name: Pumpkin smoothie
sips.how: A spoon of 100% pumpkin puree stirred into a spoon of plain unsweetened Greek yogurt and a little water.
sips.note: Not pie filling. Never a yogurt with xylitol. Skip the yogurt if dairy upsets them.

sips.name: Broth sip
sips.how: A spoon of plain chicken broth with no onion or garlic, if your vet is fine with it.

sips.name: Running water
sips.how: Cats drink more from moving water. A small fountain beats a still bowl.
